bug_title: [rejected AI] Config.from_prefixed_env raises TypeError when scalar and nested environment variables share a prefix
bug_body:
### Describe the bug

`Config.from_prefixed_env()` raises an unhandled `TypeError` when environment variables contain both a scalar configuration key and a nested configuration key sharing the same prefix.

The method supports nested configuration using double underscores (`__`). However, when a scalar key is processed first, the nested key attempts to assign into that scalar value instead of a dictionary, causing the method to crash.

### To reproduce

```python
import os
from flask import Config

config = Config(root_path=".")

os.environ["FLASK_TEST"] = "hello"
os.environ["FLASK_TEST__INNER"] = "world"

config.from_prefixed_env("FLASK")
```

### Expected behavior

The configuration loader should handle conflicting scalar and nested keys gracefully, either by resolving the conflict consistently or raising a clear, intentional configuration error.

### Actual behavior

The method raises an unhandled exception:

```text
TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
```

The exception occurs at:

```python
current[tail] = value
```

in `src/flask/config.py`, inside `Config.from_prefixed_env()`.

### Environment

- Flask: 3.2.0.dev0 (local development checkout)
- Python: 3.12.10
- Operating system: Windows

### Additional evidence

The issue was reproduced using a minimal standalone Python script. The full Flask test suite passes (491 passed, 3 skipped), indicating that this edge case is not currently covered by the existing tests.

bug_title: 3.2: update_template_context is missing from the subclass shim
bug_body:
Environment:

- Python version: 3.14.4
- Flask version: 3.2.0.dev0 (commit d086db8)

The 3.2 changelog says:

> Many ``Flask`` methods involved in request dispatch now take the current
> ``AppContext`` as the first parameter. If subclasses were overriding these
> methods, the old signature is detected, shows a deprecation warning, and will
> continue to work during the deprecation period.

As far as I can tell `update_template_context` isn't covered by that. Its
signature did change:

- 3.1.3: `def update_template_context(self, context: dict[str, t.Any]) -> None:`
- main: `def update_template_context(self, ctx: AppContext, context: dict[str, t.Any]) -> None:`

and `templating.py` now calls `app.update_template_context(ctx, context)`. But
the tuple in `Flask.__init_subclass__` (app.py, around line 258) has 12 methods
in it and `update_template_context` isn't one of them. The list you posted on
#5815 has 13, so I'm guessing it just got missed.

So a subclass that overrides it the old way gets no warning and no wrapping:

```python
from flask import Flask, render_template_string


class App(Flask):
    def update_template_context(self, context):
        context["x"] = "y"


app = App(__name__)


@app.route("/")
def index():
    return render_template_string("{{ x }}")


app.test_client().get("/")
```

```
  File "flask/templating.py", line 125, in _render
    app.update_template_context(ctx, context)
TypeError: App.update_template_context() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given
```

The request comes back as a 500 and no DeprecationWarning is raised. The same
code returns 200 on 3.1.3.

One other thing I ran into while testing this, which is probably worth its own
issue: overrides that do use the new signature but don't spell it exactly the
way the check expects are picked up as the old signature instead. Renaming the
parameter (`def dispatch_request(self, context)`) or annotating it as
`ctx: AppContext | None` makes the ctx argument get stripped, so those fail
with a TypeError as well. Same with `finalize_request` annotated
`typing.Optional[AppContext]`. Happy to file that separately if you'd rather.

bug_title: [rejected AI] `register_blueprint()` silently ignores the host option
bug_body:
`app.register_blueprint(bp, host="a.localhost")` doesn't error and doesn't do anything, because the `host` kwarg goes into `**options` and is never read, so every rule of the blueprint is registered hostless.
I checked `flask/(sansio)/blueprints.py` in 2.3.3, 3.1.3 and current `main`: `host` has never been read on that path, in any release. It just does not exist for blueprints themselves.

Depending on the app config this fails in two opposite ways, both silent.

```python
import flask

a_bp = flask.Blueprint("a_bp", __name__)
b_bp = flask.Blueprint("b_bp", __name__)


@a_bp.route("/")
def a_home():
    return "a_bp view: meant for a.localhost only"


@b_bp.route("/")
def b_home():
    return "b_bp view: meant for b.localhost only"


def probe(app):
    client = app.test_client()
    for host in ("a.localhost", "b.localhost", "evil.example"):
        r = client.get("/", headers={"Host": host})
        body = repr(r.get_data(as_text=True)) if r.status_code == 200 else ""
        print(f"GET /  Host: {host:14} -> {r.status_code} {body}")


app = flask.Flask(__name__, static_folder=None)
app.register_blueprint(a_bp, host="a.localhost")
app.register_blueprint(b_bp, host="b.localhost")

host_matched = flask.Flask(__name__, host_matching=True, static_folder=None)
host_matched.register_blueprint(a_bp, host="a.localhost")
host_matched.register_blueprint(b_bp, host="b.localhost")

print("=== host_matching=False (default) ===")
probe(app)
print("=== host_matching=True ===")
probe(host_matched)
```

Output, Flask 3.1.3 / Werkzeug 3.1.8 / Python 3.12:

```
=== host_matching=False (default) ===
GET /  Host: a.localhost    -> 200 'a_bp view: meant for a.localhost only'
GET /  Host: b.localhost    -> 200 'a_bp view: meant for a.localhost only'
GET /  Host: evil.example   -> 200 'a_bp view: meant for a.localhost only'
=== host_matching=True ===
GET /  Host: a.localhost    -> 404
GET /  Host: b.localhost    -> 404
GET /  Host: evil.example   -> 404
```

With the default app the host isn't part of matching at all, so a_bp's hostless rule answers every hostname and b_bp is registered but unreachable. This is a cross-host leak with no error, no warning, and nothing for a type checker to catch, since `**options` accepts anything.
While with `host_matching=True` it flips the other way: a hostless rule matches nothing, so everything 404s.

For contrast, `flask.Blueprint("a", __name__, host=...)` does raise a `TypeError` because it accepts some kwargs but not `host` (since it has no **options catch-all).

Some context: #5411 was closed as not planned on the basis that `register_blueprint(a_bp, host=...)` was the existing way to do this, and the example posted in reply there was never answered. Running that example is what led me here. I also posted a shorter version of this on discussion #5413 yesterday, which was removed when the discussion was closed. I'm sorry I revived a very old discussion, and that it was necessary to remove the comment. The point of it was to confirm that the report still reproduces and to contribute a tested example.
I hope that opening this issue is the correct way to proceed now.

As for what to do about it: given how subtle the interaction between `SERVER_NAME`, `host_matching` and `subdomain_matching` has historically been (see for example #5553 and the fix in #5634), I can understand not wanting to grow that API surface.
The minimal fix would then be to reject `host` loudly in `BlueprintSetupState`, same as the constructor does.

But if honoring it is on the table instead, the gap it would fill is easy to state: having `host=` for blueprints too, not only route decorators. Today, pinning more than one route to a host means repeating `host=` on each of them (and not missing any), or subclassing. To me, the missing blueprint-level scope is a feature gap, but a documented per-route recipe would already be an improvement.

Either way, the docs gap stands on its own: the blueprints page documents subdomains at blueprint scope but never says a word about hosts, which is part of why I thought `host=` was supported. I can contribute a recipe for pinning a blueprint to one host with today's API, something like this (simplified from what I run in production, together with `host_matching=True`):

```python
class HostBlueprint(flask.Blueprint):
    def __init__(self, *args, host: str, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self._host = host

    def add_url_rule(self, rule, endpoint=None, view_func=None, **options):
        options.setdefault("host", self._host)
        return super().add_url_rule(rule, endpoint, view_func, **options)
```

I can send a PR for whichever direction sounds right to you.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.13
- Flask version: 3.1.3

bug_title: `add_url_rule` leaves a route registered even after an endpoint conflict
bug_body:
## Description
‘add_url_rule’ correctly raises an error when an endpoint already exists and you try to register a different view function with the same endpoint.

However, after you catch the error and continue running the code, the URL you tried to add (/b, for example) still exists. When a user requests /b, it is routed to the view function that was already registered for that endpoint, rather than the new view function whose registration failed.

## Example

```python
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

def first():
    return "first"

def second():
    return "second"

app.add_url_rule("/a", endpoint="same", view_func=first)

try:
    app.add_url_rule("/b", endpoint="same", view_func=second)
except AssertionError as e:
    print(e)

client = app.test_client()

print(client.get("/a").status_code, client.get("/a").data)
print(client.get("/b").status_code, client.get("/b").data)
```

### Expected Result

```text
View function mapping is overwriting an existing endpoint function: same
200 b'first'
404 ...
```

### Actual Result

```text
View function mapping is overwriting an existing endpoint function: same
200 b'first'
200 b'first'
```

I think Flask correctly rejects the view-function overwrite, but the failed registration has already added the URL rule.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.11.2
- Flask version: 3.1.3

bug_title: `stream_with_context`: abandoned generator leaves the app context current on the worker thread; later requests skip `teardown_appcontext`
bug_body:
`stream_with_context` pushes the request's contexts onto whichever thread iterates the response body, and pops them only if the generator completes or is closed on that same thread. When a client disconnects mid-stream, the server abandons the body iterator and GC finalizes it later — often on a different thread. That cross-context pop fails (`LookupError`/`ValueError` from `ContextVar.reset`, swallowed as "Exception ignored in ..."), and the app context stays current on the worker thread.

Because `RequestContext.push` reuses an ambient app context of the same app, every later request on that pooled thread runs under the stuck context and `teardown_appcontext` never fires for it. Anything keyed to the app context then leaks once per thread for the life of the process — with Flask-SQLAlchemy that is one connection held idle-in-transaction per poisoned thread, with nothing in the logs.

Related: #5774 fixed the same cross-context token failure for async views; #5804 covers teardown ordering in the 3.1.2 rewrite. Neither covers the abandonment case. The docs mention that headers/session need care with `stream_with_context`, but not that a disconnect can leave the context stuck on the thread — a warning there would be helpful even if the behavior itself is hard to change.

## Reproduction

One long-lived "worker" thread serves two requests; the abandoned body iterator is GC-finalized on the main thread in between (in real deployments the reference is dropped by server machinery outside the worker — servers may never call `close()` on the iterator after a disconnect):

```python
import gc
import queue
import threading

from flask import Flask, Response, stream_with_context
from flask.globals import _cv_app

app = Flask(__name__)
teardowns = []

@app.teardown_appcontext
def note_teardown(exc):
    teardowns.append(threading.current_thread().name)

@app.route("/stream")
def stream():
    def gen():
        for i in range(100):
            yield f"chunk{i}\n"
    return Response(stream_with_context(gen()))

@app.route("/plain")
def plain():
    return "ok"

abandoned = queue.Queue()   # holds the dropped iterator, like server machinery
step2 = threading.Event()

def worker():
    # --- request A: streaming response, client disconnects after one chunk ---
    with app.test_request_context("/stream"):
        rv = app.full_dispatch_request()
    body = iter(rv.response)
    next(body)   # first chunk: stream_with_context pushes app+request ctx HERE
    abandoned.put((body, rv))   # server-side reference outlives the request
    del body, rv
    print("A: ambient ctx after abandonment:", _cv_app.get(None))

    step2.wait()  # main thread GC-finalizes the generator meanwhile

    # --- request B: any later request on this pooled worker thread ---
    print("B: ambient ctx at request start:", _cv_app.get(None))
    teardowns.clear()
    with app.test_request_context("/plain"):    # reuses the ambient ctx of the
        app.full_dispatch_request()             # same app -> no fresh app ctx
    print("B: teardown_appcontext ran for B:", bool(teardowns))
    print("B: ambient ctx after B finished:", _cv_app.get(None))

t = threading.Thread(target=worker, name="wsgi-worker-0")
t.start()

abandoned.get()          # take the reference, then drop it on the MAIN thread
gc.collect()             # generator finalized here -> cross-context pop fails
step2.set()
t.join()
```

Output (Flask 3.1.3, Python 3.13):

```
Exception ignored in: <generator object stream_with_context.<locals>.generator at 0x...>
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../flask/helpers.py", line 130, in generator
    with app_ctx, req_ctx:
  File ".../flask/ctx.py", line 284, in __exit__
    self.pop(exc_value)
  File ".../flask/ctx.py", line 264, in pop
    ctx = _cv_app.get()
LookupError: <ContextVar name='flask.app_ctx' at 0x...>
A: ambient ctx after abandonment: <flask.ctx.AppContext object at 0x10b49c830>
B: ambient ctx at request start: <flask.ctx.AppContext object at 0x10b49c830>
B: teardown_appcontext ran for B: False
B: ambient ctx after B finished: <flask.ctx.AppContext object at 0x10b49c830>
```

## Expected behavior

Request B runs under its own app context and `teardown_appcontext` fires when it finishes. Instead it silently runs under request A's leaked context, teardown never runs, and the thread stays poisoned indefinitely.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.13 (also reproduced on 3.11)
- Flask version: 3.1.3. The `main` branch (3.2-dev, post-#5639 merged context) looks affected as well: `stream_with_context` there enters the single context via `with ctx:` around the priming `yield None`, so the context is pushed at creation and only exited when the generator completes or is closed.

bug_title: AI junk
bug_body:
## Summary

`Config.from_prefixed_env` can raise an uncaught `TypeError` when an environment
variable creates a scalar configuration value and another variable later tries
to use that same value as a nested mapping.

### Reproduction

With Flask's development source at commit
`6a2f545bfd8ed31e19066a299296917e034aca58`:

```bash
FLASK_FOO=bar FLASK_FOO__BAR=baz python - <<'PY'
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)
app.config.from_prefixed_env()
PY
```

The call raises:

```text
TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
```

### What happens

`from_prefixed_env` processes matching environment variables in sorted order.
The first variable sets `config["FOO"]` to the string `"bar"`. When processing
`FLASK_FOO__BAR`, the nested traversal reaches this value and then attempts to
assign through it:

```python
current = current[part]
...
current[tail] = value
```

The intermediate value is a string rather than a mapping, so configuration
loading fails with a low-level `TypeError`.

Relevant source at the reproduction commit:
<https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/6a2f545bfd8ed31e19066a299296917e034aca58/src/flask/config.py#L172-L183>

### Expected behavior

Configuration loading should not fail with an implementation-level
`TypeError` for a prefix collision. The behavior should be defined and
deterministic, for example by rejecting the conflicting configuration with a
clear error, or by documenting and implementing precedence/merge semantics.

### Impact

An application can fail during startup or configuration initialization when
environment variables are assembled from multiple sources and a scalar key
and nested key happen to share a prefix. This can be difficult to diagnose
because the error does not identify the conflicting environment variables.

### Suggested regression test

Add a test covering both `FLASK_FOO=bar` and `FLASK_FOO__BAR=baz`, and assert the
chosen behavior for the scalar/nested conflict. If the intended behavior is to
reject the configuration, the error should identify the conflicting path.

### Environment

- Flask source commit: `6a2f545bfd8ed31e19066a299296917e034aca58`
- Flask version: `3.2.0.dev`
- Python: `3.13.13`
- Reproduction is independent of operating system semantics because it only
  relies on the environment-variable traversal logic.

I have not assigned a CWE classification. This is reported as a configuration
robustness and error-handling issue rather than a nullability finding.

bug_title: jsonify emits NaN and Infinity, which are not valid JSON
bug_body:
`jsonify` serialises `float("nan")` and `float("inf")` as the bare literals `NaN` and `Infinity`. Those are not valid JSON (RFC 8259 allows only decimal numbers), so the response is served as `application/json` but cannot be parsed by a strict parser, including the browser's `JSON.parse`.

This inherits from `json.dumps`, whose `allow_nan` defaults to `True`. `DefaultJSONProvider` sets `default`, `ensure_ascii` and `sort_keys`, but never touches `allow_nan`, so the permissive default applies.

The path to it is ordinary: any average, ratio or division that can meet an empty input produces `nan` without anything looking wrong on the server.

Replication:

```python
from flask import Flask, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/stats")
def stats():
    values = []
    mean = sum(values) / len(values) if values else float("nan")
    return jsonify({"count": len(values), "mean": mean})

with app.test_client() as c:
    r = c.get("/stats")
    print(r.headers["Content-Type"])      # application/json
    print(r.get_data(as_text=True))       # {"count":0,"mean":NaN}
```

The response advertises `application/json` with a 200, but the body is not JSON:

```python
import json
json.loads('{"count":0,"mean":NaN}')      # accepted, Python is permissive by default
json.loads('{"count":0,"mean":NaN}',
           parse_constant=lambda x: (_ for _ in ()).throw(ValueError(x)))
# ValueError: NaN     <- what a strict parser, and JSON.parse in a browser, does
```

So the failure surfaces in the client rather than the server, which makes it awkward to trace back.

Expected: either the same behaviour with it documented, or serialisation raises so the problem shows up server-side, where `ValueError: Out of range float values are not JSON compliant: nan` names the cause immediately.

There is currently no class attribute for this, although the plumbing already works, since `dumps` forwards `**kwargs` to `json.dumps`:

```python
app.json.dumps({"a": float("nan")}, allow_nan=False)
# ValueError: Out of range float values are not JSON compliant: nan
```

`DefaultJSONProvider` exposes `sort_keys`, `ensure_ascii` and `compact` as class attributes, so an `allow_nan` attribute alongside them would fit the existing pattern and let applications choose, without changing the default for anyone. I could not find `NaN` mentioned in the `DefaultJSONProvider` or `flask.json.dumps` docstrings, so at minimum a documentation note seems worthwhile.

Happy to send a PR for whichever you prefer, an `allow_nan` provider attribute or just the docs.

Environment:

- Python 3.14
- Flask 3.1.3
- Werkzeug 3.1.8

bug_title: register_blueprint name override bypasses dot validation
bug_body:
The `Blueprint` constructor explicitly prevents dots in names (`if "." in name: raise ValueError`) because dots denote nested blueprints. However, `app.register_blueprint(..., name="...")` doesn't enforce this check on the overridden name.

If a blueprint is registered with a dot via the `name` kwarg, it bypasses the restriction. This tricks the framework into treating it as a nested blueprint, causing the parent's callbacks (like `before_request`) to unexpectedly execute for the unrelated child blueprint.

### How to replicate the bug
```python
import flask

app = flask.Flask(__name__)
parent = flask.Blueprint("parent", __name__)
child = flask.Blueprint("child", __name__)

parent.before_request(lambda: setattr(flask.g, "hit", True))
child.add_url_rule("/", "index", lambda: str(hasattr(flask.g, "hit")))

app.register_blueprint(parent)
app.register_blueprint(child, name="parent.fake") # Bypasses dot validation

print(app.test_client().get("/").get_data(as_text=True))

bug_title: multiple teardown errors are discarded on Python < 3.11
bug_body:
Markdown
On Python versions prior to 3.11, `_CollectErrors.raise_any()` (in `src/flask/helpers.py`, line 682) only re-raises the very first collected error, silently swallowing any subsequent teardown errors. This makes debugging secondary teardown failures impossible on Python < 3.11.

### How to replicate the bug
1. Create a `_CollectErrors` context manager.
2. Trigger multiple teardown exceptions (e.g., DB close fails, then Cache flush fails).
3. Call `raise_any()`. Only the first exception is raised; the others are silently lost.

**Minimal Reproducible Example:**
```python
import sys

class _CollectErrors:
    def __init__(self):
        self.errors = []

    def __enter__(self):
        pass

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
        if exc_val is not None:
            self.errors.append(exc_val)
        return True

    def raise_any(self, message: str) -> None:
        if self.errors:
            if sys.version_info >= (3, 11):
                raise BaseExceptionGroup(message, self.errors)
            else:
                raise self.errors[0]   # BUG: only first error raised

collect = _CollectErrors()

with collect:
    raise RuntimeError("DB connection close failed")
with collect:
    raise ValueError("File handle close failed")

try:
    collect.raise_any("Teardown errors")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Raised: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
    print(f"Total collected: {len(collect.errors)}")
```

Expected behavior
Even without BaseExceptionGroup (which is 3.11+), subsequent errors should not be silently discarded. They should ideally be chained or at least logged before raising the first error.

Proposed Fix
Consider chaining the exceptions or logging the secondary ones before raising the first on Python versions < 3.11.

Environment:

Python version: < 3.11 (e.g., 3.10)

Flask version: 3.2.0.dev (flask-main branch)

bug_title: Config.from_file() silently ignores fewer OSError codes than from_pyfile()
bug_body:
## Summary

`Config.from_file()` and `Config.from_pyfile()` behave inconsistently when `silent=True` and an `OSError` is raised.

`from_pyfile()` silences errors for these `errno` codes:

```python
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR, errno.ENOTDIR):
    return False
```

But `from_file()` only silences:

```python
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR):
    return False
```

It is missing `errno.ENOTDIR`.

## Reproduction

`ENOTDIR` is raised when a path component is a regular file, not a directory. For example, if `/tmp/myconfig` is a regular file and you try to open `/tmp/myconfig/settings.json`, the OS raises `ENOTDIR` (not a directory).

```python
import os, tempfile
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

# create a file where we expect a directory
with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False, suffix="cfg") as f:
    f.write(b"")
    tmp = f.name

# from_pyfile with silent=True returns False (correct)
result = app.config.from_pyfile(tmp + "/nested.cfg", silent=True)
# from_file with silent=True raises OSError instead of returning False (bug)
result = app.config.from_file(tmp + "/nested.json", load=json.load, silent=True)
```

## Expected behavior

Both methods should return `False` when `silent=True` and the path is not reachable due to `ENOTDIR`, just like they both return `False` for `ENOENT` and `EISDIR`.

## Fix

Add `errno.ENOTDIR` to the tuple in `from_file()`:

```python
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR, errno.ENOTDIR):
    return False
```

bug_title: Add a built-in is_safe_redirect() helper to handle browser URL normalization (backslash → forward slash)
bug_body:
Modern browsers normalize backslashes in navigation URLs (e.g., `\\evil.com`) into forward slashes (`//evil.com`). This creates a discrepancy between how Flask/Werkzeug evaluates redirect targets and how user agents ultimately interpret them.

A common pattern used by Flask developers to prevent protocol-relative redirects is:

```python
if not url.startswith("//"):
    return redirect(url)
```

However, the following payload bypasses this logic:

```
\\evil.com
```

Flask/Werkzeug evaluates this as a safe relative path (`startswith("//") == False`), while browsers normalize it to:

```
https://evil.com
```

and perform an external redirect. This normalization behavior is consistent across Chrome, Firefox, and Safari.

As Flask does not provide a built-in redirect validation helper, developers routinely implement ad-hoc string checks that do not account for browser normalization rules, resulting in an ecosystem-wide class of open-redirect flaws.

**Feature Request**

Introduce an official, browser-aware redirect safety utility in Flask or Werkzeug, similar to Django’s `is_safe_url`, to standardize redirect validation across the framework. The helper should:

1. Normalize backslashes to forward slashes before validation.
2. Reject protocol-relative URLs (`//example.com`).
3. Optionally enforce allowed host checks.
4. Provide a documented, recommended pattern for safe redirects.

**Rationale**

- This issue is not a flaw in Flask’s redirect implementation but a recurring security footgun for developers due to inconsistent handling between application logic and browser URL normalization.
- Providing an official helper reduces the likelihood of open-redirect vulnerabilities in applications built on Flask.
- This is framework hardening rather than a security bug report, and it aligns with the expectations set by other frameworks that offer standardized redirect-safety utilities.

This feature would give developers a reliable and recommended approach to validating redirect targets securely, reducing reliance on fragile custom logic.

bug_title: Support for all methods in @app.route
bug_body:
By default, `@app.route` sets `methods` to support only `GET` requests and the [documentation](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/api/#flask.Flask.route) suggests that the parameters are then passed to `Rule`, where `methods=None` allows all methods to be used. In reality, even explicit `None` is treated as a default value and gets overwritten by `["GET"]`. I suggest adding a way to allow all methods by explicitly passing `None`.

This feature would allow more direct control over `Rule` parameters when using `@app.route`, only using defaults when no value was provided. It is currently possible to work around the issue by creating the `Rule` directly, but it would be more convinient to have that option with `@app.route` decorators. It would also remove some confusion, as `None` being treated the same way as no value by `@app.route` while having a special meaning in `Rule` seems like a bug.

bug_title: Config.from_file() missing ENOTDIR in silent error handling
bug_body:
## Description

`Config.from_file()` is missing `errno.ENOTDIR` in its silent error handling, while `Config.from_pyfile()` correctly includes it.

In `from_pyfile` (line ~193):
```python
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR, errno.ENOTDIR):
```

In `from_file` (line ~239):
```python
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR):
```

The `ENOTDIR` case was added to `from_pyfile` in PR #2581 (fixing issue #2545), but the fix was never applied to `from_json` (now `from_file`), even though the original issue title mentioned "from_json, etc."

## Reproduction

When a component of the config file path is a regular file rather than a directory (e.g., `~/.myapp` is a file, and you try to load `~/.myapp/config.toml`), `from_file()` with `silent=True` raises `OSError` with `errno.ENOTDIR` instead of silently returning `False`.

```python
import flask
import tomllib

app = flask.Flask(__name__)
# If ~/.myapp is a regular file, this raises instead of returning False
app.config.from_file("~/.myapp/config.toml", load=tomllib.load, text=False, silent=True)
```

## Expected Behavior

`from_file(..., silent=True)` should return `False` when a path component is not a directory, matching the behavior of `from_pyfile(..., silent=True)`.

## Environment

- Flask version: 3.1.x / main branch

bug_title: asgiref fails with gevent patching
bug_body:
When `gevent.monkey.patch_all()` is used, `async def` functions fail when multiple concurrent requests are sent. asgiref gives the error `RuntimeError: You cannot use AsyncToSync in the same thread as an async event loop - just await the async function directly.`. This suggests that somehow, gevent is causing a running loop to be visible across threads.

```python

gevent.monkey.patch_all()

import asyncio

from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.get("/")
async def hello_world():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
    return f"Hello, World!"
```

fix_title: clarify async view incompatibility with gevent monkey patching
fix_diff:
## 文件: docs/async-await.rst
@@ -29,6 +29,62 @@ well as all the HTTP method handlers in views that inherit from the
     runtime, greenlet>=1.0 is required. When using PyPy, PyPy>=7.3.7 is
     required.
 
+Async Views and gevent
+----------------------
+
+Flask supports defining async view functions using ``async def``, which are executed using
+:mod:`asyncio`. When running Flask under a WSGI server, async views rely on an internal
+bridge (``Flask.async_to_sync``) to integrate asyncio-based code into the synchronous request
+lifecycle.
+
+When using ``gevent``, especially with ``gevent.monkey.patch_all()``, there are important
+limitations to be aware of.
+
+Incompatibility with gevent monkey patching
+^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+
+``gevent.monkey.patch_all()`` modifies parts of the Python standard library, including
+threading and selectors, to use gevent’s cooperative greenlet-based scheduling. This
+conflicts with assumptions made by :mod:`asyncio`, which expects a single event loop per
+OS thread and threads created via :class:`threading.Thread` to be backed by real OS threads.
+
+After monkey patching, threads may instead be implemented as greenlets running on the same
+OS thread. Under concurrent requests, this can cause :mod:`asyncio` to detect multiple
+event loops in the same thread, resulting in runtime errors such as::
+
+    RuntimeError: You cannot use AsyncToSync in the same thread as an async event loop
+
+This issue typically does not appear when handling a single request, but manifests under
+concurrent load, which can make it difficult to detect during development.
+
+Unsupported configuration
+^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+
+Running Flask async views together with gevent monkey patching is **not supported**. Even
+in cases where simple async view functions appear to work, the behavior can be unreliable
+and may break under concurrency, different event loop implementations (such as ``uvloop``),
+or on different platforms.
+

bug_title: Teardown handler chain exception handling
bug_body:
Flask executes registered teardown handlers (used for closing DB connections, releasing locks, etc.) in a chain. The do_teardown_request method which is supposed to make these teardown requests does not wrap individual handlers in a try/except block. If one handler raises an exception, the loop terminates immediately, and all subsequent handlers are skipped, this can lead to the application to skip critical cleanup routines if a non critical one fails.

Sample reproduction code
```python
import threading
import time
import requests
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

#a simulation of a limited resource pool
mock_db_connections = 0

@app.route('/')
def index():
    global mock_db_connections
    mock_db_connections = mock_db_connections + 1
    return "Request Processed"

#simulating a critical teardown handler which is supposed to free resources from the db
@app.teardown_request
def critical_db_close(exc):
    global mock_db_connections
    mock_db_connections = mock_db_connections - 1

#teardown handler which can crash
@app.teardown_request
def buggy_extension(exc):
    raise Exception("Crash in buggy extension!")

def run_server():
    #just for clearner output
    import logging
    log = logging.getLogger('werkzeug')
    log.setLevel(logging.ERROR)
    app.logger.disabled = True
    
    app.run(port=5000, threaded=True)

def verify_bug():
    
    print(f"Initial DB Connections: {mock_db_connections}")
    
    try:
        requests.get('http://127.0.0.1:5000/')
    except Exception:
        pass

    #wait time to ensure teardown has happened in the other thread
    time.sleep(1)
    
    print(f"Final DB Connections: {mock_db_connections}")
    
    if mock_db_connections > 0:
        print("Teardown Chain Broken")
    else:
        print("Failed to reproduce")

server_thread = threading.Thread(target=run_server, daemon=True)
server_thread.start()
verify_bug()
```

bug_title: Proposal: CLI command to validate API endpoints by making test requests
bug_body:
### Motivation

When working on Flask applications with many API endpoints, it is sometimes
useful to quickly check whether all registered routes can be accessed without
raising unexpected errors (e.g. unhandled exceptions, 500 errors).

At the moment, developers typically need to write custom scripts or tests to
perform this kind of basic validation. Providing an opt-in CLI command could
help improve developer experience, especially during local development.

### Proposal

Introduce an optional Flask CLI command (for example, `flask check-endpoints`)
that iterates over registered routes and makes test requests using Flask’s
test client.

The goal would not be full correctness testing, but a lightweight sanity check
to detect obvious runtime errors.

Possible initial scope:
- Only routes with simple methods (e.g. GET by default)
- Skip routes with required path parameters
- Report endpoints that raise exceptions or return 5xx responses
- Development-only usage

### Design considerations

- The command should be fully opt-in and not affect existing behavior.
- No network requests; use Flask’s built-in test client.
- Keep output simple and readable (similar to `flask routes`).
- Advanced features (custom payloads, auth, etc.) could be out of scope initially.

### Open questions

- Should this live as a core CLI command or as an optional extension?
- How should endpoints with required parameters or authentication be handled?
- Should the command fail on the first error or report all failures?

Feedback on the general direction and scope would be appreciated before
starting an implementation.

bug_body:
### Description

I propose to add a "copy to clipboard" button next to all code blocks in the Flask documentation. This will allow users to easily copy example code or command-line snippets with a single click instead of manually selecting the text. This feature greatly improves usability and convenience, especially on mobile devices.

Flask documentation uses Sphinx for static site generation, and there is an existing Sphinx extension called [sphinx-copybutton](https://sphinx-copybutton.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) that provides this functionality out of the box. It can be enabled by simply adding it to the `extensions` list in the Sphinx `conf.py` file.


This extension also supports stripping common prompts (like `>>>`, `$`) from copied content, making the copied snippets cleaner.

### Problem this resolves

Currently, users have to manually select and copy code blocks, which can be error-prone and inconvenient. Adding a copy button makes the process faster and less error-prone.

### Additional notes

- The change is additive and does not affect existing documentation content or structure.
- This enhancement aligns Flask docs with modern documentation practices seen in many popular projects.

I am happy to implement this feature and create a pull request once the issue is approved.

bug_title: deprecate `should_ignore_error`
bug_body:
This was added in f1918093ac70d589a4d67af0d77140734c06c13d as part of the original code to keep the context around for use in the debugger, tests, etc. It was not part of a PR, and there's no linked issue or explanation on why it was added.

The method is only documented in the API, not in any other pages. There's no test for it. I have a feeling this isn't used. It results in an extra function call every single request, only to always return false. This can be deprecated then removed.

bug_title: `flask.testing` misleadingly appears to import `TestResponse`
bug_body:
`testing.py` contains the following:
```python
if t.TYPE_CHECKING:  # pragma: no cover
    from werkzeug.test import TestResponse
```
As such, any IDE or static checker will consider this to be valid code:
```python
import flask.testing as _flask_test

def my_test_helper(flask_test_client: _flask_test.FlaskClient) -> _flask_test.TestResponse:
    ...
```

However, at runtime, this code will fail, because `TestResponse` is not actually imported into the `flask.testing` namespace.

Possible solutions:
- Move `from werkzeug.test import TestResponse` outside the `if t.TYPE_CHECKING` block; you're already importing `werkzeug.test` in that file anyway
- Remove `from werkzeug.test import TestResponse` entirely and replace `TestResponse` with `werkzeug.test.TestResponse` in type-hints
- Change `from werkzeug.test import TestResponse` to `from werkzeug.test import TestResponse as _TestResponse`; the leading underscore signals marks the import as private, at which point it doesn't matter if its really imported or not because nobody should be using it from outside the file

bug_title: Session is not updated on redirect target endpoint in tests
bug_body:
Hello team.
During writing tests, I noticed a strange session behavior.

I want to verify that after a redirect, the target location sets valid session properties, and it seems like in tests, the session properties when following redirects are not saved/exposed to the test environment.

Here's an example:
```python
import pytest
from flask import Flask, redirect, session

@pytest.fixture
def app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.debug = True
    app.secret_key = 'test_secret'  # noqa: S105 – fake secret key for testing purposes

    @app.get('/redirect')
    def do_redirect():
        print("Redirecting to target endpoint", flush=True)
        session["redirected"] = "true"
        return redirect('/target', 302)

    @app.get('/target')
    def target():
        print("Target endpoint reached", flush=True)
        session['foo'] = 'bar'
        return 'Target', 200

    return app

@pytest.fixture()
def client(app):
    return app.test_client()

def test_session(client):
    with client:
        response = client.get("/redirect", follow_redirects=True)

        print(f"Session after a redirect: {session.items()}", flush=True)
        assert response.status_code == 200
        assert response.data == b"Target"

        assert session.get("redirected") == "true"
        assert session.get('foo') == 'bar'

        client.get("/target", follow_redirects=True)
        assert session.get('foo') == 'bar'
        assert response.data == b"Target"
        print(f"Session after a direct request: {session.items()}", flush=True)
```

The test fails on the first assertion `assert session.get('foo') == 'bar'`. 
If I comment it out, the test output is the following:

```

bug_title: Looser type annotations for send_file() path_or_file argument
bug_body:
`path_or_file` argument of `flask.helpers.send_file` is typed as `os.PathLike[t.AnyStr] | str | t.BinaryIO`. This prevents passing some objects that are `t.IO[bytes]`, but not `t.BinaryIO`. The underlying`werkzeug.utils.send_file` already allows `t.IO[bytes]` due to pallets/werkzeug#2209 since version 2.0.2.


Reproduction:
```python
from tempfile import NamedTemporaryFile
from typing import IO

from flask.helpers import send_file


# The return type cannot be "BinaryIO" because "NamedTemporaryFile" is incompatible with it according to Mypy.
def some_function() -> IO[bytes]:
    file = NamedTemporaryFile()
    ...
    return file


file = some_function()
send_file(file)
```

Raises the following exception with Mypy 1.16.1.
```
error: Argument 1 to "send_file" has incompatible type "IO[bytes]"; expected "PathLike[str] | str | BinaryIO"  [arg-type]
```

I could simply change the return value of `some_function` to `_TemporaryFileWrapper[bytes]` or cast it to `BinaryIO`.
However, I would like to allow `t.IO[bytes]`.

Side note: `_TemporaryFileWrapper[bytes]` conforms to `PathLike[str]` due to python/typeshed#7840. That is why it is accepted by `flask.helpers.send_file`.

Allowing `t.IO[bytes]` would be backwards compatible change as all `t.BinaryIO` are also `t.IO[bytes]`.
[Mypy Playground](https://mypy-play.net/?mypy=latest&python=3.10&gist=4d7e2a43a847df9d332f5b7daba7a9fe)

bug_title: document that `request.full_path` leaves query string percent encoded
bug_body:
WHAT IS THE BUG?

`request.full_path` is documented as *“Requested path as unicode, including the query string.”*  
However, Werkzeug URL-unquotes only the **path** (before “?”); the **query string** is returned **raw**.  
Code that searches or whitelists on `full_path` can therefore be bypassed by percent-encoding a slash inside a parameter.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

HOW TO REPLICATE

```
```python
from flask import Flask, request
app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/show_picture")
def show_picture():
    # naïve traversal filter
    if "../" in request.full_path:
        return "Blocked", 400
    return f"full_path = {request.full_path}", 200

# run:  flask --app poc run


# bypass: "../" hidden as "%2F"
curl "http://127.0.0.1:5000/show_picture?img=..%2F..%2Fetc%2Fpasswd"
Result → 200 OK; the filter misses the traversal because ../ appears as ..%2F.
```

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------


EXPECTED BEHAVIOR
Documentation (and the full_path docstring) should warn clearly:

"Only the portion before “?” is URL-unquoted. The query string is returned raw; unquote it manually (e.g. urllib.parse.unquote_plus) before using it for validation or filtering."

Without that notice, filters like

if "../" in request.full_path:
    ...
if request.full_path.startswith("/admin"):
    ...

can be bypassed with %2F inside the query string.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Python version: 3.12.3

Flask version: 2.3.3

Werkzeug version: 3.1.3

OS: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Discovery: Jefferson Gozanels GHomez
Proof-of-concept & report: Sebastián Alba Vives

bug_title: The `template_filter` decorator doesn't work if you don't pass an argument
bug_body:
## What's the issue?

You can use `template_filter` as a decorator, but it only registers the filter if you write an explicit name or an empty set of parentheses. If you call it without parens, the filter doesn't get registered.

It's a small difference and can be confusing.

## Minimal example

Consider the following program:

```python
from flask import Flask, render_template_string


app = Flask(__name__)


@app.template_filter
def double(x):
    return x * 2


@app.route("/")
def index():
    return render_template_string("2 times 2 is {{ 2 | double }}")
```

If you run this app (`flask run --port 8008 --debug`) and then open it in your browser (`http://localhost:8008`) you'll get an error:

```
jinja2.exceptions.TemplateAssertionError: No filter named 'double'.
```

This is confusing, and it took me a while to realise the missing parentheses in `app.template_filter` were at fault.

## Suggested fix

I think it would be helpful if the decorator either:

* Supported being called without parentheses, or
* Printed an explicit warning if called this way, e.g. `Did you use 'template_filter' as a decorator without parentheses? You need to call it with 'template_filter()'`

bug_title: Reference cycle caused by exception handling
bug_body:
A reference cycle is introduced by Flask's exception handling mechanism. Specifically, the exception object retains a reference to the stack frame, which in turn holds a reference back to the exception. This creates a reference cycle between the traceback and the exception instance.

This becomes particularly problematic in applications where the garbage collector is disabled (gc.disable()). Even when the GC is enabled, this cycle puts unnecessary pressure on memory management.

The issue originates from the following line in the Flask source code: https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/9225f8bb28d291b1610c8a58e3233aa6bbdc1808/src/flask/app.py#L1507

The fix is simple: the reference to the exception object should be explicitly released once it is no longer needed.

A minimal reproducible example demonstrating this issue can be found here:
👉 https://github.com/tomasz-pankowski/exception-memory-leak/tree/main

Environment:

- Python version: any
- Flask version: 3.1.0 (earlier ones too)

bug_title: int route converters are actually uint, but not documented as such
bug_body:
In #2643, a user noted that flask routes with an `int` converter only accepts unsigned integers.

I'll summarize a few different opinions and options in that thread:
1. a user can create their own converter that accepts unsigned integers, or modifies the existing converter (but only on their codebase). An example code snippet was provided in the issue.
2. The user's report could be treated as a bug in the `int` converter, so the fix would be to modify the flask `int` converter to accept the other ~50% of legitimate integers. Assumptions were made about which part of the integer space most people would use. Concerns were raised about how users may be relying on this bug, and that it should not be fixed for fear of breaking said users.
3. The user's report could be treated as a bug in the documentation, so a presumed fix would be to amend [the documentation](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/api/#url-route-registrations) which currently states "The following converters are available: [...] `int`: accepts integers"; it could be changed to "`int`: accepts _unsigned_ integers".

My expectation would have been that either option 2 or 3 would be selected, but instead it appears that the issue was locked to further comment and no further action was taken. So, the documentation is still at odds with the behavior of flask vs the math and computer science definition of integer. I'm not wedded to either solution, but would the pallets team be open to implementing a fix in either direction?

Thank you,
-Andrew

It makes an already confusing topic more complicated to explain: app context is active for requests and cli commands, don't push an app context before making a request, etc.

I think merging the two contexts could be possible. The single context (`ExecutionContext`?) would have the `g`, `request`, and `session` attributes, but accessing `request` or `session` when not in a request would raise an error.

from flask import Flask


Flask("x").config.update({"A": "3"})  # 'Type of "update" is partially unknown - reportUnknownMemberType'

Based on other typing in the same class, it looks like it could be:
```python
class Config(dict[str, t.Any]):

bug_body:
The tests runned with `pytest` works with python3.11 and not in 3.12:

How to reproduce:
```
git clone git@github.com:pallets/flask.git
cd flask/examples/tutorial
python3.11 -m venv venv3.11
python3.12 -m venv venv3.12
# install dependencies
# setup db
```
In both cases, the webservice runs properly with `./venv3.1x/bin/flask --app flaskr run --debug`.

However, running the tests show different results. In `venv3.11`, the 24 tests are green. In `venv3.12` virtualenv, there is 6 failures (and 18 green). The failures are due to a `DeprecationWarning` which becomes an error:
```
DeprecationWarning: The default timestamp converter is deprecated as of Python 3.12; see the sqlite3 documentation for suggested replacement recipes
```

The full output is provided at the end of the bug report.

The `DeprecationWarning` is documented in the [3.12 release](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.12.html): '[default adapters and converters](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#sqlite3-default-converters) are now deprecated. Instead, use the [Adapter and converter recipes](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#sqlite3-adapter-converter-recipes) and tailor them to your needs.' Copy-pasting blindly the recipes in `tests/conftest.py`, `flaskr/__init__.py` and `flaskr/db.py` does not fix the errors.

The errors can be fixed by adding thoses lines in conftest.py:
```python
def convert_timestamp(val):
    """Convert Unix epoch timestamp to datetime.datetime object."""
    return datetime.datetime.strptime(val.decode("utf-8"), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S").replace(tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc)

sqlite3.register_converter("timestamp", convert_timestamp)

bug_title: `pyright` type checking seems to be unused. `mypy` still being used.
bug_body:
We added `pyright` in 3.0.3 (see: https://github.com/pallets/flask/pull/5457), but `mypy` is still being used for type checking https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/main/tox.ini#L29-L32, and `pyright` is not.

If this was an intentional change of type checkers, then would expect that `mypy` be completely removed, and `pyright` be the command run in `tox typing`.

It should be noted, however, that running `pyright` yields 90 errors (71 tests/19 src). Is there an upgrade path or was this an oversight?

Environment:

- Python version:
- 3.12
- Flask version:
- 3.0.3
fix_title: git add tox.ini requirements/typing.txt
fix_diff:
## 文件: tox.ini
@@ -27,8 +27,8 @@ skip_install = true
 commands = pre-commit run --all-files
 
 [testenv:typing]
-deps = -r requirements/typing.txt
-commands = mypy
+deps = pyright
+commands = pyright
 
 [testenv:docs]

bug_title: Flask incorrectly parses chained query parameters
bug_body:
When accessing the /test route with both category and location query parameters (http://localhost:5000/test?category=fish&location=water), Flask correctly parses category but ignores location.

### Steps to Reproduce
Access the URL http://localhost:5000/test?category=fish&location=water.
Expected behavior: Both category and location parameters should be correctly parsed by Flask.
Actual behavior: Flask parses category correctly ("excavator"), but location is ignored.

```(python)
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/test")
def test():
    category = request.args.get("category")
    location = request.args.get("location")
    return {"category": category, "location": location}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(debug=True)
```

Expected:
```(json)
{
    "category": "fish",
    "location": "water"
}
```

Got:
```(json)
{
    "category": "fish",
    "location": null
}
```
### Environment:

- Python version: 3.8.10
- Flask version: 3.0.3

bug_title: Document behaviour of __init__ in cli.prepare_import()
bug_body:
The code in [cli](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/main/src/flask/cli.py#L215) is a bit confusing: if you have an __init__ file in the project it causes the cli to step out of the directory and import it from outside the directory.

E.h. I was working in directory /Users/visgean/p/social-flask/chapter2/models_app and the flask run command tried to import the app as chapter2.models_app.app, which did not work:

```
Error: While importing 'chapter2.models_app.app', an ImportError was raised:
```

I had to dig into the code to see that the solution is to delete the init file, apparently i am not the only one: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/70835630/while-importing-myapp-app-an-import-error-was-raised


I think this feature is a bit undcomented and to be honest I am not sure what the goal is. If I run flask run in a directory I dont want it to work at all with the parent directory. E.g. flask should only be aware of the current directory.

Proposed fixes: 
- Specifically mention this behavior on start e.g. "importing app as chapter2.models_app.app due to presence of __init__.py"
- Mention this behaviour in docs somewhere
- Remove this behavior unless there is a clear need for it.

This is a duplicate of #1740 — that may have been closed for lack of a clear rationale, however, and I'd like to suggest it again with the following reasoning.

The documentation currently gives this example for using `open_resource()`:

```python
with app.open_resource("schema.sql") as f:
    conn.executescript(f.read())
```

On Windows, however, this can fail to open a file encoded in UTF-8, which most are these days, and safer code looks like this:

```python
with app.open_resource("schema.sql", mode="rb") as f:
   conn.executescript(f.read().decode("utf-8"))  # type: ignore [attr-defined]
```

(The type comment is needed to prevent mypy from complaining about `f.read()` possibly being a string with no `.decode()` method, as it can't tell that the file was opened in 'rb' mode.)

It would be cleaner and more flexible to be able to write:

```python
with app.open_resource("schema.sql", encoding="utf-8") as f:
   conn.executescript(f.read())
```
